ch01.anchor: courtesy name Yingliu
ch01.note: A Chinese man of this milieu carried several names: a given name (here 仰山 Yangshan) and a formal zi or courtesy name (应骝 Yingliu) taken at adulthood and used by peers. Chen also changed his surname from Cheng (程) to Chen (陈) when he entered underground work, a common precaution; the book's title and this translation use the revolutionary name throughout.

ch01.anchor: held the metropolitan degree
ch01.note: The jinshi, the highest degree in the imperial civil-service examinations and the gateway to senior office. A salt commissioner (盐政使) oversaw the lucrative state salt monopoly; the grandfather's rank marks the family as one of real standing before its decline.

ch01.anchor: Commentary on the Water Classic
ch01.note: The Shuijing zhu, a celebrated early-sixth-century work by Li Daoyuan expanding a terse older gazetteer of China's rivers into a vast topographical and folkloric survey. Citing it lends the local lake an ancient pedigree.

ch01.anchor: the filial daughter Cao E
ch01.note: A classic tale of filial devotion. The historical Cao E stele (曹娥碑) is real and famous, chiefly for a riddling inscription later added to it; the drowning legend is traditional rather than documented. Cao'e, the girl's name, was in time given to the river and the county town themselves.

ch01.anchor: national salvation through industry
ch01.note: Shiye jiuguo, the early-twentieth-century conviction that China could be saved by building modern commerce and industry rather than by politics. Chen's abandonment of it for revolution is the arc of this chapter; the parallel slogan 'salvation through education' appears below.

ch01.anchor: the May Fourth Movement broke out in 1919
ch01.note: The student-led protests of May 4, 1919, against the Versailles award of German concessions in Shandong to Japan, which swelled into a nationwide movement for cultural renewal and against imperialism and warlordism. It is conventionally taken as the seedbed of Chinese Communism.

ch01.anchor: the notorious February 7 Massacre
ch01.note: The Erqi incident of February 7, 1923: the warlord Wu Peifu, of the Zhili clique that then controlled the Beijing-Hankou line, crushed the railwaymen's strike by force. It became a founding martyrdom of the Chinese labor movement. The casualty figures here are the book's.

ch01.anchor: more than two thousand li of it
ch01.note: The li is a traditional Chinese unit of distance, in the modern period standardized at half a kilometer; two thousand li is roughly a thousand kilometers, about the length of the Beijing-Hankou line.

ch01.anchor: the magazine China Youth
ch01.note: Zhongguo qingnian, launched in 1923 as the organ of the Socialist Youth League and edited by Yun Daiying, among the most influential progressive periodicals of its day among young readers.

ch01.anchor: the Socialist Youth League of China
ch01.note: The Communist Party's youth organization, founded 1922, from which promising members like Chen graduated into full Party membership; the forerunner of today's Communist Youth League.

ch01.anchor: the League Central secretary, Ren Bishi
ch01.note: Ren Bishi (1904-1950), then a very young secretary of the Youth League's central committee, later one of the five top leaders of the CCP alongside Mao, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai and Zhu De.

ch01.anchor: the death of Lenin
ch01.note: Lenin died on January 21, 1924; memorial issues of the Chinese left press introduced many young readers, Chen among them, to the Soviet model as a template for China's own revolution.

ch01.anchor: a captive of Chu
ch01.note: The closing image of Yun Daiying's prison poem. 'A captive of Chu' (Chu qiu) is a classical byword, from the Zuo zhuan, for a prisoner who keeps his dignity and loyalty in captivity. The book reproduces the poem in Zhou Enlai's own 1953 hand and prints it as shown here; other published texts of the poem read slightly differently in two characters, a variation left as the book gives it.

ch01.anchor: the May Thirtieth Movement
ch01.note: The nationwide anti-imperialist upheaval of 1925, touched off by the events this section narrates: British-officered police in Shanghai's foreign settlement shooting Chinese demonstrators. It marks the high tide of the mid-1920s revolution.

ch01.anchor: the International Settlement
ch01.note: The foreign-run enclave in central Shanghai, outside Chinese jurisdiction, administered by the Shanghai Municipal Council (the 工部局) with its own police force and, for cases involving Chinese, the Mixed Court. That an armed foreign administration policed Chinese streets is the standing grievance behind this whole episode.

ch01.anchor: the council's chief inspector, McEuen
ch01.note: K. J. McEuen, Commissioner of the Shanghai Municipal Police in 1925. His order to fire and the killings that followed on Nanjing Road on May 30 made him a lasting symbol of the settlement's use of force against Chinese; he was later removed amid the outcry.

ch01.anchor: carried the Northern Expedition victoriously into Hubei
ch01.note: The Northern Expedition (1926-1928), the Kuomintang-Communist military campaign out of Guangdong to defeat the northern warlords and reunify China; its early advance into the central provinces frames much of this chapter's action.

ch01.anchor: the April 12 counter-revolutionary coup
ch01.note: On April 12, 1927, Chiang Kai-shek turned on his Communist allies in Shanghai, massacring Communists and labor activists with gangster help and ending the first Kuomintang-Communist united front. The 'white terror' (白色恐怖) that follows in the book is the term for the wave of arrests and killings across the country afterward.

ch01.anchor: an armed uprising at Nanchang
ch01.note: The Nanchang Uprising of August 1, 1927, the Communists' first armed revolt against the Kuomintang after the split; its date is now marked as the founding day of the People's Liberation Army. He Long, then a Kuomintang general, was one of its commanders, which is why he was hunted afterward.

ch01.anchor: a reward of 100,000 silver dollars
ch01.note: The silver dollar (dayang) was the standard hard currency of Republican China; a hundred thousand of them was an enormous bounty, a measure of how badly the Kuomintang wanted He Long.

ch01.anchor: societies and secret sects of men like Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng
ch01.note: Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng were the bosses of Shanghai's Green Gang, the criminal fraternity that ran the city's underworld and that Chiang Kai-shek used as muscle in the April 12 purge; secret sects (会道门) were popular quasi-religious brotherhoods.

ch01.anchor: working in the Central Special Branch
ch01.note: The Zhongyang teke, the CCP's clandestine intelligence and security service in Shanghai, set up under Zhou Enlai after the 1927 split to protect the underground, gather intelligence, and punish traitors. It is the world in which the rest of this book unfolds, and Chen Yangshan's life's work.

ch01.anchor: the traitor Gu Shunzhang
ch01.note: Gu Shunzhang, a senior Special Branch operative whose capture and defection in April 1931 exposed much of the CCP underground and led directly to the deaths of many, including Yun Daiying. His name recurs through this book as its great catastrophe.

ch01.anchor: the Municipal Council's four proposals
ch01.note: Four by-laws the Shanghai Municipal Council put before the 1925 ratepayers' meeting, among them a press-registration rule widely read as censorship and a rise in wharfage dues. Chinese residents, who paid the settlement's rates but had no vote in it, fought the proposals as a further tightening of foreign control, which is why they loom so large here.

ch01.anchor: in the foothills of the Kuaiji range
ch01.note: The Kuaiji (Guiji) range, south of Hangzhou Bay, is among the anciently storied mountains of China: the legendary sage-king Yu the Great is said to be buried there, and it was nearby, at the Orchid Pavilion in 353 CE, that the calligrapher Wang Xizhi held his celebrated gathering.

ch01.anchor: came originally from Huizhou prefecture in Anhui
ch01.note: Huizhou, in southern Anhui, was the home of the Huizhou merchants (徽商), one of imperial China's two great merchant networks and a byword for commercial wealth married to Confucian respectability — the standing this declining family had once had.

ch01.anchor: moved during the Xianfeng years to Shaoxing prefecture
ch01.note: Shaoxing, in eastern Zhejiang, is an old water town famous for its rice wine and, in this period, for supplying the empire's offices with legal secretaries (绍兴师爷); it is also the birthplace of the writer Lu Xun. The Xianfeng years (1851–1861) were the reign in which the Taiping wars raged.

ch01.anchor: was a failed licentiate
ch01.note: The xiucai or 'licentiate' was the lowest imperial examination degree, won at the county level; it brought gentry standing and exemption from corporal punishment but no office or income. Chen's father held it and rose no higher, hence 'a poor scholar.'

ch01.anchor: an apprentice at a money shop in Wuhan
ch01.note: Wuhan is the conurbation of three towns where the Han River meets the Yangtze: Wuchang on the south bank (the old administrative city), with Hankou and Hanyang opposite, Hankou being the great commercial port. A 'money shop' (钱庄) was a traditional Chinese private bank.

ch01.anchor: During the Taiping upheaval
ch01.note: The Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864), a vast religious-political civil war against the Qing led by Hong Xiuquan, who proclaimed a 'Heavenly Kingdom' at Nanjing. Perhaps twenty million died before it was crushed; the family fled its reach into Zhejiang.

ch01.anchor: On February 7 the warlords Cao Kun and Wu Peifu
ch01.note: Cao Kun (1862–1938) headed the Zhili clique of Beiyang warlords and, notoriously, bought the presidency of the Republic in 1923 by bribing the parliament; Wu Peifu was his chief general and the real power on the Beijing-Hankou line.

ch01.anchor: the Communist Lin Xiangqian
ch01.note: Lin Xiangqian (1892–1923), a locomotive worker and union leader at Jiang'an, killed as the passage describes. With Shi Yang he became one of the founding martyrs the February 7 strike gave the labor movement.

ch01.anchor: Shi Yang, legal adviser
ch01.note: Shi Yang (1889–1923), a Wuhan lawyer who defended workers without fee and counseled the railway unions; executed on February 15, 1923. He is remembered as the movement's 'labor lawyer' (劳工律师).

ch01.anchor: joined with the Chinese Kuomintang under Sun Yat-sen
ch01.note: Sun Yat-sen (1866–1925), leader of the 1911 revolution that overthrew the Qing and founder of the Kuomintang, revered by Nationalists and Communists alike as father of the Republic. His 1924 policy of alliance with the Communists and Soviet Russia made the united front of these years possible.

ch01.anchor: built a revolutionary united front
ch01.note: The First United Front (1924–1927): on Sun Yat-sen's initiative and with Soviet advice, Communists joined the Kuomintang as individuals to make a common revolution against the warlords. Its violent collapse in 1927 is the hinge of this whole chapter.

ch01.anchor: chief political instructor at the Whampoa Military Academy
ch01.note: The Whampoa (Huangpu) Military Academy, founded near Guangzhou in 1924 with Soviet help to officer the united front's army. Chiang Kai-shek was its commandant and Zhou Enlai headed its political department; its graduates went on to lead both the Nationalist and the Communist armies.

ch01.anchor: He was a reader of New Youth
ch01.note: New Youth (新青年), the journal Chen Duxiu founded in 1915 that led the New Culture Movement — championing plain-language writing, science, and democracy, and after 1919 Marxism. It was the intellectual seedbed of the May Fourth generation.

ch01.anchor: Chen Tanqiu took Chen Yangshan aside
ch01.note: Chen Tanqiu (1896–1943), a Hubei teacher who was one of the thirteen delegates to the CCP's First Congress in 1921; executed in Xinjiang in 1943.

ch01.anchor: where Xiang Ying relayed
ch01.note: Xiang Ying (1898–1941), a Wuhan textile worker who rose high in the Party and the labor movement; later political commissar of the New Fourth Army, killed in 1941 after the New Fourth Army (Anhui) Incident.

ch01.anchor: Lin Yunan, secretary of the Wuhan district committee
ch01.note: Lin Yunan (1898–1931), whose full life the book gives below, was a leading labor organizer. He would be among the twenty-four Communists shot together at Longhua in Shanghai on February 7, 1931 — the 'Longhua martyrs,' a disaster traced to Gu Shunzhang's betrayal.

ch01.anchor: an older cousin of Lin Biao
ch01.note: Lin Biao (1907–1971), later one of the Communists' foremost commanders, a marshal, and Mao Zedong's designated successor — until he died in a plane crash in 1971 while, by the official account, fleeing a failed coup. The family gave several sons to the revolution.

ch01.anchor: together with He Mengxiong
ch01.note: He Mengxiong (1898–1931) and Li Qiushi (1903–1931), Communist labor and youth leaders, died with Lin Yunan among the Longhua Twenty-Four; He Mengxiong had just before opposed the Party leadership's ultra-left line.

ch01.anchor: Yang Xingfo spoke first
ch01.note: Yang Xingfo (Yang Quan, 1893–1933), an American-trained scientist and associate of Sun Yat-sen, later secretary of the China League for Civil Rights; assassinated by Kuomintang agents in 1933.

ch01.anchor: the Japanese cotton mills in Qingdao and Shanghai
ch01.note: The Japanese-owned cotton mills, of which the Naigai Wata (内外棉) company ran some of the largest in Shanghai, were centers of the worst industrial conditions and of the labor struggles that led to the May Thirtieth Movement.

ch01.anchor: The Communist Gu Zhenghong, in the front rank
ch01.note: Gu Zhenghong (1905–1925), a Communist worker at a Naigai mill shot dead by a Japanese overseer on May 15, 1925; his killing was the spark that lit the May Thirtieth Movement two weeks later.

ch01.anchor: and Liu Hua, chairing the meeting
ch01.note: Liu Hua (1899–1925), a young Communist and leader of the West Shanghai workers; seized during the movement by the Settlement's police and secretly put to death in December 1925.

ch01.anchor: along the roads of the International Settlement
ch01.note: Nanjing Road, where the shooting below took place, was and is Shanghai's chief commercial street, running through the heart of the International Settlement; the massacre there on May 30, 1925, gave the movement its name.

ch01.anchor: poured toward the Louza patrol house
ch01.note: The Louza (Laozha, 老闸) police station on Nanjing Road, from which the Settlement's British-officered police opened fire on the crowd demanding the arrested students' release.

ch01.anchor: the printing workers of the Zhabei district of Shanghai, led by Chen Yun
ch01.note: Chen Yun (1905–1995), then a young printing worker and union organizer, later one of the most powerful leaders of the People's Republic and the principal architect of its planned economy.

ch01.anchor: made up of Zhou Enlai, Wang Yifei, Nie Rongzhen
ch01.note: Nie Rongzhen (1899–1992), later a marshal of the People's Liberation Army and the director of China's nuclear-weapons program. Yan Changyi (1898–1929), a military organizer, was executed in Shanghai in 1929.

ch01.anchor: Comrades Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Chen Yannian
ch01.note: Mao Zedong (1893–1976), the future leader of the People's Republic, was then a rising Party organizer of the peasant movement. Zhou Enlai (1898–1976), who in these years ran the Party's Shanghai underground and its Special Branch, is the presiding figure of this whole book and Chen Yangshan's ultimate chief.

ch01.anchor: the Fengtian warlord Zhang Zuolin
ch01.note: Zhang Zuolin (1875–1928), the 'Old Marshal,' warlord ruler of Manchuria and head of the Fengtian clique, who then held Beijing. He had the Party's co-founder Li Dazhao hanged in 1927 and was himself killed the next year by a Japanese bomb.

ch01.anchor: Li Dazhao, Zhao Shiyan, Chen Yannian
ch01.note: Leading Communists killed in the 1927 terror. Li Dazhao (1889–1927), co-founder of the Party with Chen Duxiu, was hanged in Beijing by Zhang Zuolin; Chen Yannian (1898–1927) was Chen Duxiu's elder son; Zhao Shiyan, Xiao Chunü, Wang Shouhua, and Xiong Xiong were labor and youth leaders executed in Shanghai and elsewhere.

ch01.anchor: the treachery of Chiang Kai-shek and Wang Jingwei
ch01.note: Chiang Kai-shek (1887–1975), commandant of the Whampoa academy and commander of the Northern Expedition, who broke with the Communists in April 1927, led the Nationalist government thereafter, and after 1949 ruled Taiwan. His fellow-'traitor' here is Wang Jingwei (see below).

ch01.anchor: The general secretary, Chen Duxiu, was removed
ch01.note: Chen Duxiu (1879–1942), founder of New Youth and co-founder and first general secretary of the CCP. Blamed for the catastrophe of 1927 as 'right opportunism' — for subordinating the Party to the Kuomintang — he was removed here and later expelled; the charge is the Party's own framing of a defeat with many authors.

ch01.anchor: of five men: Zhang Tailei, Zhou Enlai, Li Lisan
ch01.note: The provisional leadership after Chen Duxiu's fall. Zhang Tailei (1898–1927) would die weeks later leading the Guangzhou Uprising; Li Lisan gave his name to the reckless 'Li Lisan line' of 1930; Zhang Guotao later rivaled Mao and in 1938 defected to the Nationalists; Li Weihan long served in the leadership.

ch01.anchor: He Long, Zhu De, Ye Ting, Liu Bocheng
ch01.note: The commanders of the Nanchang Uprising, all later giants of the Communist army. He Long and Zhu De (a founder and commander-in-chief of the Red Army) became marshals; Ye Ting led the uprising's troops and later the New Fourth Army; Liu Bocheng, the 'One-Eyed Dragon,' became a marshal and the army's leading strategist.

ch01.anchor: after the Party's August 7 Conference
ch01.note: The emergency conference of August 7, 1927, which met after the united front's collapse, ousted the Chen Duxiu leadership for good, put Qu Qiubai at the head, and set the Party on the course of armed uprising and land revolution. Mao Zedong's saying that 'political power grows out of the barrel of a gun' was uttered here.

ch01.anchor: Qu Qiubai held that He Long
ch01.note: Qu Qiubai (1899–1935), essayist and Party leader who headed the CCP after the August 7 Conference; captured and executed by the Nationalists in 1935, leaving a famous, unsparingly self-doubting last testament.

ch01.anchor: the situation in western Hunan, He Long said
ch01.note: Western Hunan (Xiangxi), the rugged, ethnically mixed border country that was He Long's home ground, where he now proposed to raise a force; it became the nucleus of the Hunan-western-Hubei revolutionary base.

ch01.anchor: settled He Long together with Zhou Yiqun
ch01.note: Zhou Yiqun (1896–1931), He Long's close comrade and co-founder with him of the Honghu base in the Hunan-Hubei lake country; killed in 1931.

ch01.anchor: and He Long, Guo Liang, Xu Teli
ch01.note: Among the nucleus were veterans of standing: Xu Teli (1877–1968), a schoolmaster who had taught the young Mao Zedong and joined the Party at fifty, and Guo Liang (1901–1928), a Hunan labor leader soon executed by the Nationalists.

ch01.anchor: on November 17 with Liu Bocheng and Lin Boqu
ch01.note: Lin Boqu (1886–1960), a founding elder of the Party (one of the 'Five Elders' of Yan'an) and later a senior statesman of the People's Republic.

ch01.anchor: guarded by Lu Dongsheng
ch01.note: Lu Dongsheng (1908–1945), a former oil-mill hand who became He Long's bodyguard and in time a general; he died in an accident in 1945.

ch01.anchor: Luo Qingchang wrote an essay in his memory
ch01.note: Luo Qingchang (1918–2014), a career intelligence officer who worked under Zhou Enlai and eventually headed the Party's Central Investigation Department; his memorial essay lends this account both its insider authority and its partisan warmth.

ch01.anchor: a Kuomintang member (of the left) named Bao Junfu
ch01.note: Bao Junfu (also known as Yang Dengying, 1900–1969), the Kuomintang intelligence man whom Chen Yangshan would later turn into one of the Communists' most valuable double agents inside the enemy's secret service — a story the chapters ahead tell.

ch01.anchor: arrested by a British constable at the Ewo cotton mill
ch01.note: The Ewo (Yihe, 怡和) mill belonged to Jardine, Matheson & Co., the great British trading house of the China coast; the arrest was made by a constable of the foreign Settlement's own police.

ch01.anchor: on the execution ground at Yuhuatai in Nanjing
ch01.note: Yuhuatai ('Terrace of the Rain of Flowers'), a hill just south of Nanjing that the Nationalist government used as an execution ground; great numbers of Communists and others were shot there, and it is now a memorial park.

ch01.anchor: gave his life at Longhua in Shanghai
ch01.note: Longhua, on Shanghai's southern edge, held the garrison headquarters and its killing ground; the twenty-four Communists shot here on February 7, 1931, Lin Yunan among them, are honored as the Longhua Martyrs.

ch01.anchor: director of the general investigation bureau of the Jin-Sui Border Region
ch01.note: The Jin-Sui (Shanxi-Suiyuan) Border Region was a Communist base on the north China frontier during the war against Japan, where Chen Yangshan ran intelligence under He Long — the wartime posting the book's later chapters reach.

ch01.anchor: escort Comrade He Long smoothly to the Honghu region
ch01.note: Honghu (Hong Lake), the marshy lake country on the Hunan-Hubei border where He Long and Zhou Yiqun built their soviet base after 1928.

ch01.anchor: the revolutionary masses in the days of the great revolution
ch01.note: 'The Great Revolution' (大革命) is the standard Chinese name for the national revolutionary upheaval of 1924–1927 — the united front, the mass movements, and the Northern Expedition — brought down by the 1927 split.

ch01.anchor: a member of the National Revolutionary Military Commission of the Soviet areas
ch01.note: The 'Soviet areas' (苏区) were the rural base areas the Communists governed as local soviets — workers'-and-peasants' councils on the Russian model — after 1927; the Jiangxi Soviet was the largest.
